nameStory: The 'rusty' in this lichen's name comes from its distinctive reddish-brown to rust-colored appearance when wet or mature. It earned the 'brook' part of its name because it's almost always found near or partially submerged in clean, flowing water. The scientific name 'lacustris' means 'of lakes,' though this lichen is more commonly found along streams and brooks than in still lake waters.
description: Rusty Brook Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms thin patches on rocks in and around clean streams and brooks. It appears as a rusty reddish-brown to dark brown crust that seems almost painted onto wet rocks. The patches are typically small, rarely exceeding a few inches across, and have a smooth to slightly bumpy texture. This is one of the few lichens that can tolerate being periodically submerged in flowing water.

idTips.label: Aquatic habitat
idTips.description: Always found on rocks that are in or very close to clean, flowing water - often getting splashed or briefly submerged

idTips.label: Rust-brown color
idTips.description: Distinctive reddish-brown to dark rust color, especially noticeable when wet - feels smooth and slightly slippery to touch

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Forms a thin, flat crust that adheres tightly to rock surfaces - difficult to scrape off with a fingernail

idTips.label: Small patches
idTips.description: Creates small, irregular patches usually 1-3 inches across that may merge with neighboring colonies

idTips.label: Rock substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on hard, non-calcareous rocks like granite, schist, or quartzite in stream beds

habitat: Look for Rusty Brook Lichen on rocks in clean, fast-flowing streams and brooks throughout New England's forested areas. It prefers hard, acidic rocks like granite and schist that are regularly wetted by spray or brief submersion. This lichen indicates excellent water quality, so you'll find it in pristine mountain streams and unpolluted woodland brooks.

seasonality.spring: Most visible during spring snowmelt when streams are running high and the lichen is frequently wetted, showing its richest rust-brown colors.
seasonality.summer: Still present but may appear duller during dry periods when water levels drop and the lichen dries out more frequently.
seasonality.fall: Becomes more prominent again as autumn rains increase stream flow and keep the lichen moist and colorful.
seasonality.winter: Often hidden under ice or snow, but can sometimes be seen along ice-free sections of fast-moving streams where it maintains its dark coloration.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a living water quality indicator - it's so sensitive to pollution that scientists use its presence to certify that a stream has pristine water conditions, making it more reliable than many expensive testing instruments!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with wet, rusty-looking iron stains on rocks, but unlike mineral stains, this lichen has slightly raised edges and a more uniform, organic-looking texture. Memory trick: if it looks too perfectly rust-colored and evenly distributed, it's probably the lichen, not actual rust!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name referencing brooks, the scientific name 'lacustris' means 'of lakes,' which can be confusing since this species is rarely found in lake environments. This naming confusion arose from early misidentification of specimens, but the brook-focused common name is much more accurate for where you'll actually encounter this species.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ionaspis species commonly found in New England, compare it with other aquatic lichens in the Hymeneliaceae family like Hymenelia species. Rusty Brook Lichen is distinguished by its consistently rust-brown color and preference for flowing rather than still water, while Hymenelia lichens tend to be grayer and can tolerate more varied moisture conditions.
